old: Indirect object pronouns answer the question 'to whom?' or 'for whom?' an action is performed. They are placed immediately before conjugated verbs.
new: You know me, te and le from *me gusta* and *me duele* (Units 22 and 21). Indirect object pronouns answer the question 'to whom?' or 'for whom?' an action is performed. Like the direct pronouns of Unit 12, they are placed immediately before conjugated verbs.
why: screen presents me/te/le as new; gustar (Unit 22) and doler (Unit 21) taught them

old: Master indirect object pronouns: me, te, le, nos, les.
new: Use indirect object pronouns: me, te, le, nos, les.

old: How to tell direct and indirect objects apart:\n• Direct Object (DO): The thing or person directly affected. Question: ¿Qué? (What?) or ¿A quién? (Whom?). Pronouns: lo, la, los, las.\n• Indirect Object (IO): The recipient. Question: ¿A quién le...? (To/for whom?). Pronouns: le, les (me, te, nos).
new: You know lo, la, los, las from Unit 12 and le, les from the last lesson. How to tell direct and indirect objects apart:\n• Direct Object (DO): The thing, or the person the verb acts on (*Llamé a Carlos*). Question: ¿Qué? (What?). Pronouns: lo, la, los, las.\n• Indirect Object (IO): The person who receives the thing (*Le di el libro*). It usually comes with a direct object. Pronouns: le, les (me, te, nos).
why: screen presents Unit 12's lo/la/los/las as new, and its own ¿A quién? test fits the direct person (Llamé a Carlos) as well as the indirect one

old: I bought flowers → I bought them.
new: I bought flowers and took them home.

old: I bought flowers for my mother → I bought her flowers.
new: I wrote to my mother and bought her flowers.

old: I called Carlos → I called him. / I wrote to Carlos → I wrote to him.
new: I called my mother yesterday and wrote to my father.

old: I can use the test questions '¿Qué?' (direct) and '¿A quién?' (indirect) to choose pronouns.
new: I can find the direct object with '¿Qué?' and tell it from the person who receives it.
why: the test question ¿A quién? also fits a direct person (Llamé a Carlos); the lesson never practises the questions

old: I wanted to tell it to Carlos, but I forgot.
new: I wrote the letter yesterday and sent it to Carlos.

old: Master the famous Spanish phonological rule: le/les changes to 'se' before lo/la/los/las.
new: Change le/les to se before lo, la, los and las.

old: I can clarify 'a él', 'a ella', or 'a ellos' when needed for context.
new: I can choose se lo, se la, se los or se las to match the thing.
why: clarifying with 'a él/a ella' is not practised in any exercise

old: Notice the written accent: when two pronouns attach to an infinitive (dar + te + lo = dárselo), the stress stays on the infinitive vowel, requiring a written accent mark.
new: Notice the written accent: the stress stays where it was, so two pronouns on an infinitive (dar + se + lo = dárselo) and even one pronoun on a gerund (buscando + lo = buscándolo) need a written accent mark.
why: dar + te + lo gives dártelo, not dárselo; the rule left out the gerund + one pronoun that example 2 shows

why: 'leave it to me' means 'I'll handle it'; dejármelo is 'leave it with me'
